c.tagline: Ancient Indian Ocean port city rebuilding behind the world's tightest security.

taxi.fareNote: No meters; agree fare before departure. Independent taxi/tuk-tuk use by foreign visitors is strongly discouraged - nearly all visitors move only in vetted, pre-arranged vehicles with security escort.

emergency.medical: 888 (nationwide emergency line); Aden Adde Modern Hospital, Erdogan/Recep Tayyip Erdogan Hospital
emergency.note: US State Dept rates Somalia Level 4: Do Not Travel; visitors should rely on private security escorts, not public emergency services

avoid.reason: Virtually the whole city is high-risk; avoid Bakara Market and anywhere outside the secured airport (Halane) zone without professional armed escort.
Hotels, restaurants and government districts are recurring targets of al-Shabaab attacks — move only with vetted security and vary routines.

hood_desc: The old city on the Indian Ocean, a maze of coral-stone alleys, 25-plus historic mosques and the fish and produce markets; suits travelers focused on heritage and culture who accept high security caution.
The KM4 junction area, the city's busiest commercial and hotel hub with restaurants, shops and NGO offices; best for business travelers needing central access.
A southwestern residential district near Somali National University; suits longer-stay visitors, students and NGO/diaspora visitors seeking a quieter base.

The secured airport perimeter (Halane/'Green Zone') housing the airport, AU/UN compounds and the most fortified hotels; the default (and safest available) base for nearly all international visitors, officials and journalists.

water.note: Poor sanitation infrastructure makes tap water unsafe; use bottled or treated water.

transit.pay: Cash (Somali Shillings or small USD) paid directly to the driver or conductor; no cards, apps or fare cards exist. Fares are negotiated or fixed by informal local convention rather than metered.
transit.hours: Daytime only in practice; travel after dark is strongly discouraged citywide
transit.note: No formal public transit authority; minibuses and bajaj serve residents but are not recommended for foreign visitors due to security risk - nearly all international travelers use private/escorted vehicles

airport.name: Aden Adde International Airport (MGQ)
airport.drive: 15-25 min (convoy/escorted transfer standard; heavy security checkpoints add time)

tip.r: Not customary among locals but appreciated at hotels/restaurants catering to international staff; round up or add 5-10% where service was good.

food.name: Bariis iskukaris
food.desc: Somalia's festive rice: basmati cooked with xawaash spice, cardamom and stock, stained with saffron colour and heaped with goat, camel or chicken.

places.name: Village Restaurant
places.note: Mogadishu institution, long the best-known sit-down restaurant in the city.

places.name: Tufaax Restaurant
places.note: Broad Somali menu, singled out in recent listings for hospitality.

places.name: Karmel Hotel and Restaurant
places.note: Traditional Somali cooking in a modern hotel dining room.

food.name: Suqaar
food.desc: Small cubes of camel, goat or beef fried fast with onion, pepper and xawaash, then eaten with rice, pasta or folded into canjeero.

places.name: Village Restaurant
places.note: Dependable place for the classic meat-and-rice plates.

places.name: Salsabiil Restaurant
places.note: Straightforward Somali kitchen, well rated for authentic flavours.

places.name: Hamar Weyne market eateries
places.note: Small canteens in the oldest quarter cook suqaar to order all day.

food.name: Canjeero (laxoox)
food.desc: Lacy fermented sorghum pancake, the Somali breakfast staple, torn and dipped in sesame oil and sugar, or eaten with liver and tea.

places.name: Hamar Weyne market eateries
places.note: Morning stalls in the old town griddle canjeero from before sunrise.

places.name: Bakaara Market food stalls
places.note: The city's biggest market, with breakfast counters throughout.

places.name: Karmel Hotel and Restaurant
places.note: Serves the traditional breakfast spread for guests and locals alike.

food.name: Camel meat and camel liver (beerka geela)
food.desc: Camel is the prestige meat here: grilled steaks and ribs at dinner, and a breakfast fry-up of liver with onion and pepper eaten with canjeero.

places.name: Bakaara Market food stalls
places.note: Camel butchers and grill stands supply the city; earliest and freshest here.

places.name: Village Restaurant

places.name: Hamar Weyne market eateries
places.note: Old-town breakfast counters specialise in liver fried with onion.

food.name: Grilled Indian Ocean seafood
food.desc: Kingfish, tuna and lobster landed on the Benadir coast, grilled over coals with lime and chilli and served with rice and banana.

places.name: Indian Ocean Star Restaurant
places.note: Beachfront kitchen for fresh seafood with the ocean in front of you.

places.name: Beach View Restaurant
places.note: Seafood dining on the strip where Mogadishu goes out on Fridays.

places.name: Ocean View Mogadishu
places.note: Seafood with Somali seasoning, popular for sunset dinners.

food.name: Sambusa and halwo
food.desc: Crisp triangular pastries of spiced mince or lentils, and halwo, the dense cardamom-and-ghee sweet that ends every Somali celebration.

places.name: Bakaara Market food stalls
places.note: Sambusa fryers work the afternoons; halwo sold by the slab from sweet shops.

places.name: Hamar Weyne market eateries
places.note: Old-town confectioners are known for the best halwo in the city.

places.name: Tufaax Restaurant
places.note: Sambusa served as a starter with the main Somali plates.

food.name: Shaah (Somali spiced tea)
food.desc: Black tea boiled with cardamom, cinnamon, cloves and ginger, cut with milk and heavily sugared; poured from morning until late at night.

places.name: Hamar Weyne tea stalls
places.note: Street tea benches where the city's talking gets done, all day.

places.name: Bakaara Market tea stalls
places.note: Tea counters throughout the market, thick and sweet by default.

places.name: Village Restaurant
places.note: Serves the spiced tea after meals in a comfortable setting.

food.name: Caano geel (camel milk)
food.desc: Fresh camel milk, slightly salty and tangy, brought in daily from pastoral herds; drunk plain, cold, or lightly soured.

places.name: Bakaara Market milk sellers
places.note: Camel milk arrives by jerrycan each morning and sells out fast.

places.name: Hamar Weyne market eateries
places.note: Old-town counters serve camel milk with the breakfast spread.

places.name: Karmel Hotel and Restaurant
places.note: One of the sit-down places where camel milk is offered to guests.

landmarks: Mogadishu Cathedral
This bombed-out Catholic cathedral, built in 1928, stands as a hauntingly beautiful ruin overlooking the Indian Ocean, symbolizing the city's turbulent history.
Lido Beach
Mogadishu's most famous stretch of white sand and turquoise water draws crowds for swimming, football, and camel rides, especially lively during Eid celebrations.
Fakhr ad-Din Mosque
Dating to 1269, this elegant coral-stone mosque with a distinctive dome is one of the oldest surviving Islamic structures in East Africa.
Bakara Market
A sprawling, chaotic open-air bazaar and the commercial heart of the city, offering an unfiltered look at everyday Somali trade and street life.
Al-Uruba Hotel
Perched above the fishing harbor, this iconic seafront hotel offers sweeping ocean views and has long served as a gathering point for visitors.
Mogadishu Sea Port
The bustling historic harbor, lined with colorful fishing boats and dhows, remains a vital lifeline and a striking photographic backdrop of the coastline.
Villa Somalia
The fortified presidential palace complex sits atop a hill overlooking the capital, serving as the seat of government and a symbol of national sovereignty.
Aden Adde International Airport
As the gateway to Mogadishu, this coastal airport offers striking views where runways meet the Indian Ocean, often the first landmark visitors encounter.
Peace Garden
A tranquil landscaped park built as a symbol of post-conflict renewal, offering residents and visitors a rare green, relaxing public space in the capital.
Mogadishu Skyline
The evolving cityscape of whitewashed buildings, minarets, and new construction rising along the coast captures Mogadishu's resilience and ongoing rebirth.

train.note: Somalia has no working railway (colonial-era lines are long gone). All land travel is by road.

bus.note: No scheduled international coach services - land borders with Kenya and Ethiopia are effectively closed or insecure for ordinary travel. Domestic minibuses/coaches do link Mogadishu with towns such as Afgooye, Baidoa and (route conditions permitting) Kismayo, but there is no formal operator with online booking, and much of the country carries serious security warnings. Check current advice before any overland trip.

ferry.note: Mogadishu's port handles cargo, not scheduled passenger ferries. Coastal movement is by informal dhows/small boats only; there is no reliable international passenger sea service.

half.name: Marka
half.blurb: Ancient Indian Ocean port town in Somalia known for its old Swahili-influenced architecture.

full.name: Baidoa
full.blurb: Agricultural city in southern Somalia known as a regional farming center.
